findings.reason: The English title is an unqualified modern technical name, not a visibly attributed historical source heading. A synchrocyclotron is the distinct cyclotron type with approximately fixed guide B and reduced RF frequency as the relativistic revolution period increases. Here the authoritative source and the correctly rewritten body describe a fixed-ring proton synchrotron, with increasing guide B and RF tracking v/C at a fixed harmonic. The body explicitly distinguishes the modern classification, but that later distinction does not make the standalone modern title correct.

requirements.frozen_requirement: Fixed bending radius requires increasing guide B with increasing momentum; RF follows arrival phase and v/C at a fixed harmonic. Historical relativistic mass and modern momentum must be consistent with unchanged m0.
requirements.observation: The prose statement momentum = Lorentz factor * rest mass * speed is p=gamma*m0*v, equivalent to the source's historical p=m*v with m=gamma*m0. Independent transverse force balance gives p=|q|BR. Thus ramping B at fixed R is correct while m0 remains fixed. With fixed circumference C, f_rev=v/C and f_RF=h*f_rev for fixed integer h; both texts increase the RF frequency with v and describe its c-limit. Gap E points along positive-proton velocity and does positive work. No fixed-B synchrocyclotron behavior is imported into the body.

erratum_definition_basis.source_definition: One electron gains one electron-volt when traversing a one-volt accelerating potential difference.
erratum_definition_basis.constant_premise: The saved elementary-charge row is 1.602 176 634 e-19 (exact) C. The derivation uses that charge row and the definition V=J/C, not the author candidate or the saved electron-volt result as proof.
erratum_definition_basis.signed_work: Delta K=q*(V_initial-V_final). The positive energy gain uses the accelerating sense of the voltage; for a magnitude, Delta K=|q|*|Delta V|. Both candidates specify an accelerating potential difference, so the negative charge of an electron does not produce a sign error.
